system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Ventral pontine lesion causing locked-in syndrome
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Locked-in syndrome due to bilateral ventral pontine injury
mechanism: Bilateral injury to the ventral pons interrupts corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts, causing quadriplegia and anarthria. The dorsal pontine tegmentum and ascending reticular activating system are spared, preserving consciousness; vertical eye movements and blinking can also remain intact because their principal control structures are rostral to the ventral pontine lesion.
vignette: A 58-year-old man suddenly develops dysarthria followed by quadriplegia. MRI shows an acute infarction involving the ventral pons after basilar artery thrombosis. He is awake and follows commands by blinking. He cannot speak or move his limbs and has no voluntary horizontal eye movements, but he can look up and down.
lead: Which of the following patterns of neural injury best explains this patient's findings?
correct: Bilateral interruption of corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts in the ventral pons with preservation of the dorsal reticular activating system
distractors: Bilateral destruction of the dorsal pontine tegmentum including the ascending reticular activating system with preservation of corticospinal tracts
Bilateral lesions of the posterior limbs of the internal capsules with destruction of thalamocortical arousal pathways
A medial medullary lesion involving the pyramids and hypoglossal nuclei with preservation of pontine corticobulbar pathways
Bilateral anterior cingulate and medial frontal lesions causing loss of motivation with intact descending motor pathways
distractor_notes: Destruction of the ascending reticular activating system would impair consciousness, which is preserved in classic locked-in syndrome.

Bilateral internal-capsule lesions could cause severe motor deficits but do not explain the characteristic combination of pontine cranial motor dysfunction, loss of horizontal gaze, and preserved vertical eye movements.

Medial medullary lesions can injure pyramids and hypoglossal structures but do not produce the classic ventral-pontine locked-in pattern with widespread corticobulbar interruption and preserved arousal.

Bilateral anterior cingulate/medial frontal injury can cause akinetic mutism, in which initiation is impaired; the patient here is clearly conscious and attempts to communicate with vertical eye movements but is mechanically unable to move or speak.
key_expl: This is classic locked-in syndrome from a ventral pontine infarct. Bilateral corticospinal injury causes quadriplegia and corticobulbar injury causes anarthria and bulbar paralysis. The dorsal reticular activating system is spared, so consciousness is preserved. Vertical eye movements and blinking are often preserved and become the principal means of communication.
objective: Localize locked-in syndrome to bilateral ventral pontine corticospinal/corticobulbar injury with preservation of dorsal arousal pathways and vertical eye movements.
